arXiv:2607.20512v1 [cs.LG] 06 Jul 2026

The Active Ingredient in Muon’s Grokking

Yufeng Wang Affiliation: Independent Researcher Email: louiswang524@gmail.com
Abstract

The Muon optimizer reaches the grokking threshold on modular arithmetic faster than AdamW. Prior work attributes this to “spectral-norm constraints plus orthogonalized momentum,” but to better understand Muon’s behavior we isolate which of these ingredients actually matters. We run multi-seed and multi-learning-rate sweeps to decompose and stress-test the effect. First, an ablation shows the speedup comes from orthogonalization (the Newton–Schulz iteration), not spectral scaling: orthogonalize-only matches full Muon, whereas spectral-only is no faster than AdamW and is unreliable, and this verdict holds across learning rates. Second, a mechanistic analysis finds that orthogonalizing optimizers reach generalization at roughly 3×3\times lower spectral norm and, controlling for how much the embedding actually moves, settle into a lower-norm solution rather than simply perturbing the embedding less. Third, reducing the Newton–Schulz iteration count from five to one accelerates reaching the threshold but makes the grokked solution fragile, prone to transient collapse, with fragility that grows with learning rate; a single iteration is fast and stable only at small learning rate, while the canonical five iterations are the learning-rate-robust choice. We also show spectral scaling can be dropped at no measured cost. A methodological thread runs throughout: under a stability-aware metric, “faster” claims about grokking optimizers can invert, so we report both first-crossing and sustained-grok times. To support reproducibility, we release our full training and analysis code at https://github.com/louiswang524/muon-grokking-frontier.

Keywords: grokking, Muon optimizer, orthogonalization, Newton–Schulz, optimization dynamics, mechanistic interpretability.

1 Introduction

Grokking, the onset of generalization long after a model has memorized its training set (8), offers a clean probe of optimizer dynamics. 10 report that Muon (2) groks in fewer epochs than AdamW on modular arithmetic, crediting both orthogonalized momentum (a Newton–Schulz iteration) and spectral-norm-based update scaling. Which mechanism matters, why, and whether either admits improvement remain open. We answer all three in a regime where seconds-to-minutes per run make the multi-seed sweeps, learning-rate sweeps, and significance tests that separate a real effect from an artifact entirely practical.

The study doubles as a cautionary tale about how grokking speed is measured. The pre-registered metric, first step with validation accuracy at least 0.950.95, rewards optimizers that touch the threshold and then oscillate away from it. We show the hazard is not hypothetical: it inverts the apparent ranking of our own proposed variant. Every headline is therefore reported under two metrics, first-crossing and stable-grok (validation accuracy at least 0.950.95 sustained for the remainder of training).

Contributions.

(1) An ablation that isolates orthogonalization, not spectral scaling, as the ingredient behind Muon’s grokking speedup, and shows the conclusion is robust across learning rates and across modular addition, subtraction, and multiplication (§3, §5.4). (2) A mechanistic finding that orthogonalizing optimizers reach a lower-norm, Fourier-distributed solution rather than AdamW’s sparse-Fourier circuit, established with an embedding-movement control that rules out the “moves the embedding less” explanation (§4). (3) The speed–stability frontier: the Newton–Schulz iteration count and the learning rate jointly trade first-touch speed against the durability of the grokked solution, so fewer iterations help only in a bounded regime (§5). (4) A methodological point, that grokking-speed claims can silently invert between first-crossing and stability-aware metrics, with a released, deterministic reproduction harness.

2 Setup

Task. Modular addition mod p=97p{=}97 is primary; subtraction and multiplication are robustness checks (§5.4). Inputs are [a,b,=][a,b,{=}], the target is (a∘b)modp(a\circ b)\bmod p, 40%40\% of pairs train and the rest are held out. The grokked addition circuit is Fourier-based (7), giving §4 a reference.

Model. A one-layer, four-head transformer with dmodel=128d_{\text{model}}{=}128. The 2D hidden matrices receive the optimizer under test; embeddings, unembeddings, and biases use AdamW, following standard Muon practice.

Optimizer knobs. The Muon update orthogonalizes the momentum buffer with n​sns Newton–Schulz iterations, then applies it with an RMS-and-dimension scale factor (spectral_scale). We toggle each independently. Note spectral_scale is a per-matrix scalar, not a spectral-norm projection; our claim that spectral scaling is inert concerns this factor, not spectral-norm control in general.

Metrics. We report first-crossing and stable-grok steps-to-grok at the pre-registered 0.950.95 threshold. FLOPs-to-grok charges Newton–Schulz only when orthogonalization runs (a spectral-only configuration pays none), reported beside wall-clock-to-grok. Every number is a mean over at least 5 seeds; significance uses two-sample tt-tests with Holm–Bonferroni correction. Two contrasts are pre-registered as primary: orthogonalize-only vs. AdamW, and reduced-n​sns vs. canonical Muon.

Learning-rate regime. Grokking is rate-sensitive (§3.2). At lr=10−2=10^{-2} the phenomenon compresses into ∼\sim400 steps and AdamW oscillates across the threshold (58–82 post-crossing dips below 0.90.9 vs. Muon’s 11–15), so first-crossing misleads. We run the primary study at lr=10−3=10^{-3} and add a sweep over {×10−4,10−3,×10−3}\{3\!\times\!10^{-4},10^{-3},3\!\times\!10^{-3}\}.

3 Ablation: Which Ingredient?

Muon recap. For a 2D weight WW with gradient GtG_{t} and momentum μ\mu, Muon forms a momentum buffer, orthogonalizes it, and applies a dimension-dependent scale:

Bt=μ​Bt−1+Gt,Ot=NSn​s​(Bt),Wt=Wt−1−η​γ​Ot.B_{t}=\mu B_{t-1}+G_{t},\quad O_{t}=\mathrm{NS}_{ns}(B_{t}),\quad W_{t}=W_{t-1}-\eta\,\gamma\,O_{t}. (1)

Writing the buffer’s SVD as Bt=U​Σ​V⊤B_{t}=U\Sigma V^{\!\top}, orthogonalization sends Ot→U​V⊤O_{t}\to UV^{\!\top} (every singular value replaced by 11). Concretely, NSn​s\mathrm{NS}_{ns} applies n​sns quintic Newton–Schulz iterations from X0=Bt/∥Bt∥FX_{0}=B_{t}/\lVert B_{t}\rVert_{F}, Xk+1=a​Xk+b⁡(Xk​Xk⊤)​Xk+c​(Xk​Xk⊤)2​XkX_{k+1}=aX_{k}+b(X_{k}X_{k}^{\!\top})X_{k}+c(X_{k}X_{k}^{\!\top})^{2}X_{k}, driving XkX_{k} toward that polar factor U​V⊤UV^{\!\top}. The factor γ=max⁡(1,nout/nin)\gamma=\sqrt{\max(1,n_{\text{out}}/n_{\text{in}})} is the RMS-and-dimension scale (spectral_scale). Two knobs define the ablation: whether to orthogonalize (Ot=NS⁡(Bt)O_{t}=\mathrm{NS}(B_{t}) vs. raw Ot=BtO_{t}=B_{t}) and whether to apply the scale (γ\gamma as above vs. γ=1\gamma=1). The 2×22{\times}2 design gives M0–M3 below (M3 replaces the whole update with AdamW), and an n​sns sweep (§3.3) varies orthogonalization quality from none (n​s=0ns{=}0) to full.

3.1 Primary (mod-add, lr=10−3=10^{-3}, 5 seeds).

Variant Ortho (n​sns) Spectral First-cross Stable-grok FLOPs
M0 full Muon yes (5) yes 1856±1181856\pm 118 1856 (stable) 2.96e13
M1 ortho-only yes (5) no 𝟏𝟕𝟒𝟒±𝟏𝟏𝟑\mathbf{1744\pm 113} 1744 (stable) 2.78e13
M2 spectral-only no yes 3088±11073088\pm 1107 4932 (unstable) 4.69e13
M3 AdamW — — 2372±3602372\pm 360 4488 (unstable) 3.60e13

Orthogonalization is the active ingredient. Orthogonalize-only (M1) matches full Muon (M0 vs. M1: p=0.21p{=}0.21) and beats AdamW (M1 vs. M3: p=0.010p{=}0.010, primary). Spectral-only (M2) is not faster than AdamW (p=0.25p{=}0.25) and is erratic (σ=1107\sigma{=}1107). M0/M1 are stable (stable-grok == first-cross) while M2/M3 are not: orthogonalization buys a more durable grok.

3.2 Learning-rate robustness (5 variants ×\times 4 seeds ×\times 3 rates; full table in Appendix A). The ablation verdict survives: orthogonalize-only beats spectral-only at lr=10−3=10^{-3} (p=0.052p{=}0.052) and ×10−33\!\times\!10^{-3} (p=0.053p{=}0.053), and at lr=×10−4=3\!\times\!10^{-4} spectral-only groks in only 1/4 seeds while orthogonalize-only groks 4/4. The Muon-vs-AdamW first-crossing gap is more rate-dependent (significant at ×10−43\!\times\!10^{-4}, p=0.025p{=}0.025; directional at 10−310^{-3}, p=0.078p{=}0.078; closed at ×10−33\!\times\!10^{-3}), but under stable-grok Muon still beats AdamW at ×10−33\!\times\!10^{-3} (p=0.039p{=}0.039) because AdamW destabilizes as the rate rises. We claim the precise statement: Muon reaches a stable grok faster than AdamW across rates, and its first-touch advantage is largest at small rate.

3.3 Newton–Schulz sweep (lr=10−3=10^{-3}, 5 seeds). We vary the number of orthogonalization iterations n​sns (steps-to-grok, lower is faster):

Newton–Schulz iterations n​sns 0 (off) 1 3 5 (default)
first-crossing 3088 1544 2000 1856
stable-grok 4932 3136 2000 1856

More orthogonalization is not better: a single iteration reaches the threshold fastest (1544 steps, 17%17\% sooner than the default five), yet its stable grok (3136) is the worst of any n​s≥1ns{\geq}1 — the first sign of the frontier (§5). As consistency checks, n​s=0ns{=}0 (orthogonalization off) matches M2 exactly, and n​s=5ns{=}5 reproduces M0 bit-for-bit (determinism).

Takeaway. Orthogonalization, not spectral scaling, is the active ingredient, and the verdict holds across learning rates (§3.2) and operations (§5.4). Yet the non-monotonic sweep shows more orthogonalization is not strictly better—a tension we explain mechanistically in §4 and turn into a speed–stability frontier in §5.

4 Mechanism: A Lower-Norm Solution, Not Less Movement

At the grok point (averaged over seeds), the two optimizer families reach visibly different solutions:

Variant max. singular value at grok embedding Fourier spectrum
M0 full Muon 5.5 near-uniform
M1 ortho-only 6.2 near-uniform
M2 spectral-only 11.0 concentrated
M3 AdamW 15.9 concentrated

The orthogonalizing variants (M0, M1) grok at roughly 3×3\times lower spectral norm than AdamW, and keep the embedding’s frequency content spread out rather than concentrating it into a few Fourier modes the way AdamW and spectral-only do. One might object that orthogonal updates simply move the embedding less, making the uniform spectrum trivial; an embedding-movement control rules this out (Appendix C): all optimizers change the embedding by essentially the same relative amount (∥Δ​E∥/∥Einit∥≈1.0\lVert\Delta E\rVert/\lVert E_{\text{init}}\rVert\approx 1.0), yet only AdamW concentrates the spectrum, so Muon reaches a genuinely different, lower-norm solution rather than an untouched initialization. Notably the fragile n​s=1ns{=}1 variant is intermediate, drifting partway toward the concentrated code, which links the instability of §5 to a partial collapse onto the sparse-Fourier solution. (The averaged-power IPR is a coarse proxy for per-neuron analysis.)

5 The Speed–Stability Frontier

The ablation points to two levers: drop the inert spectral scaling, and reduce the Newton–Schulz count. We test the composed variant, Lean-Muon (orthogonalize-only, n​s=1ns{=}1). For continuity with §3, canonical Muon here is M0 and Lean5 is M1; small numerical differences from §3 reflect 8 seeds here versus 5 there.

5.1 Compute-matched (mod-add, lr=10−3=10^{-3}, 8 seeds).

Variant n​sns spec. First-cross Stable-grok FLOPs Wall
AdamW – – 2388±3022388\pm 302 4932 3.62e13 40.2s
Muon (canonical) 5 yes 1750±2061750\pm 206 1750 (stable) 2.79e13 33.3s
Lean5 (ortho-only) 5 no 1630±1821630\pm 182 1630 (stable) 2.60e13 30.2s
Lean1 (n​s=1ns{=}1) 1 no 𝟏𝟑𝟗𝟓±𝟏𝟗𝟔\mathbf{1395\pm 196} 3800 (fragile) 2.14e13 24.3s

Spectral scaling is removable at no cost: Lean5 matches Muon’s stability, runs directionally faster (p=0.27p{=}0.27), and costs less. Reducing n​sns trades stability for speed: Lean1 reaches 0.950.95 fastest—20%20\% sooner than canonical Muon (1395 vs. 1750, p=0.005p{=}0.005, primary, survives Holm) and 42%42\% sooner than AdamW, at 23%23\% fewer FLOPs than Muon—but on 6/8 seeds it collapses (to as low as 0.230.23–0.380.38) after first grok, so its stable grok (3800) is worse than Muon’s (1750). Fast to touch the threshold, slow to settle.

5.2 The frontier is governed by (n​sns, learning rate). Lean1 beats Muon on first-crossing at every rate (p=0.32,0.043,0.001p{=}0.32,0.043,0.001), but stability flips: at ×10−43\!\times\!10^{-4} Lean1 is faster and stable (4875 vs. 5481); at 10−310^{-3} it is fragile; at ×10−33\!\times\!10^{-3} all variants barely stabilize. The Newton–Schulz count and the learning rate jointly set a speed–stability frontier; the canonical five iterations are the rate-robust operating point.

5.3 Why approximate orthogonalization destabilizes (hypothesis). A single step under-orthogonalizes; with weight decay this appears to let the solution drift off the grokked manifold and re-collapse. Fuller orthogonalization (n​s≥3ns{\geq}3) damps the drift at the cost of a slower first crossing, predicting fragility that worsens with effective step size, consistent with §5.2.

5.4 Robustness (subtraction, multiplication; 5 seeds, 15k steps). First-crossing steps-to-grok (grok rate in parentheses):

Variant subtraction multiplication
AdamW 5850 (5/5) 2250 (5/5)
Muon (canonical) 8925 (4/5) 1850 (5/5)
Lean5 (ortho-only) 6230 (5/5) 1710 (5/5)
Lean1 (n​s=1ns{=}1) 5040 (5/5) 1390 (5/5)

Three findings replicate across all three operations: Lean1 reaches the threshold faster than canonical Muon (sub p=0.001p{=}0.001, mul p=0.030p{=}0.030, add p=0.005p{=}0.005); the speed carries the same fragility (Lean1 worst under stable-grok on each task); and dropping spectral scaling never hurts and on subtraction clearly helps (Lean5 beats Muon, p=0.021p{=}0.021). One ordering is task-dependent: canonical Muon beats AdamW on addition and multiplication but is slower on subtraction (p=0.005p{=}0.005), not because of orthogonalization but because of the spectral term it carries; the orthogonalize-only variants beat both there. The check reinforces the two recommendations.

6 Limitations and Conclusion

Limitations. One architecture, one scale, one task family, so the at-scale behavior of the frontier (where orthogonalization is not free) is untested. The first-crossing metric is unstable; we mitigate with stable-grok. §4’s Fourier claim uses a coarse proxy. Secondary contrasts that do not survive Holm correction are reported as exploratory; both primaries survive.

Conclusion. Muon’s grokking advantage comes from orthogonalization, not spectral scaling, and is robust across learning rates; the grokked solution is lower-norm. But “more is worse” is too glib: the Newton–Schulz count and the learning rate jointly govern a speed–stability frontier, and the canonical five iterations are a sensible rate-robust default. Spectral scaling, however, can be dropped for free. The broader lesson is methodological: grokking-speed claims must be made under a stability-aware metric, or they can silently invert.

Reproducibility and disclosure.

The full study is 258 runs, an estimated 3.1×10163.1\times 10^{16} FLOPs; the largest single run is 2.4×10142.4\times 10^{14} FLOPs, ∼4×105×{\sim}4\times 10^{5}\times below the Track-1 per-run cap of 102010^{20}. The released artifact (Appendix B) is bit-for-bit deterministic per seed, so any checkpoint is exactly regenerable. AI tools assisted code scaffolding and editing; all results and claims were author-verified. No conflicts or funding to declare.

Appendix B Supplementary: released artifacts

The supplementary ZIP contains: (i) per-run training logs (full validation/training accuracy and diagnostic trajectories: weight norm, max singular value, Fourier-IPR) as JSON; (ii) the deterministic data generator with seed configs and the dual-metric (first-crossing, stable-grok) measurements with FLOPs and wall-clock; (iii) the ablation, learning-rate, frontier, robustness, embedding-change, and FLOP-budget analysis scripts that regenerate every table; and (iv) the optimizer and training harness with a 28-test suite (including determinism and FLOP-accounting regression tests). No checkpoints are stored: the harness is bit-for-bit deterministic per seed (verified, M0≡\equivNS5 per seed), so any state is regenerable from the released config.

Appendix C Supplementary: embedding-movement control (§4)

To rule out that orthogonalization merely perturbs the embedding less—which would make its uniform Fourier spectrum a trivial consequence—we measure the relative embedding change ∥Efinal−Einit∥/∥Einit∥\lVert E_{\text{final}}-E_{\text{init}}\rVert/\lVert E_{\text{init}}\rVert alongside the final Fourier-IPR (mod-add, lr=10−3=10^{-3}, 4 seeds).

Optimizer relative ∥Δ​E∥\lVert\Delta E\rVert final Fourier-IPR
AdamW 0.996 0.085 (concentrated)
Muon 0.994 0.022 (uniform)
Lean5 (ortho-only) 0.994 0.025 (uniform)
Lean1 (n​s=1ns{=}1) 0.998 0.069

Every optimizer rewrites the embedding by essentially the same amount (relative change ≈1.0{\approx}1.0), yet Muon and Lean5 end Fourier-uniform while AdamW concentrates. The “moves the embedding less” explanation is therefore rejected. The fragile n​s=1ns{=}1 variant (Lean1) sits between the two, consistent with the partial-collapse account of its instability in §5.

Appendix D Extended related work

Grokking was introduced by 8; 7 reverse-engineered the Fourier-multiplication circuit we use as a reference in §4. Mechanistic accounts tie grokking to weight norm and solution efficiency: the loss-landscape / weight-norm “LU” picture of 4, the efficiency trade-off between memorizing and generalizing circuits of 11, and the adaptive-optimizer instability (“slingshot”) of 9. Our §4 (grokking at lower spectral norm) and §5 (a stability metric, and an instability that grows with learning rate) connect directly to these; the slingshot phenomenon is a close analogue of the post-grok collapses we observe for under-orthogonalized updates. Optimizer geometry. Muon (2) orthogonalizes momentum via Newton–Schulz; 1 frame such matrix-sign updates as steepest descent under a spectral norm, which motivates separating orthogonalization from the dimension scale we ablate. We contrast against AdamW (5), and note that our inert per-matrix spectral_scale factor is distinct from spectral-norm control as in 6, which we do not test. Muon and grokking. 10 reported the speedup we decompose and qualify; 3 accelerate grokking by amplifying slow gradients, a complementary mechanism.
